Up to 100% of men have microplastics in their semen

I got mine to zero. The first documented case.

A 2024 study detected microplastics in 100% of human and dog testicular tissue.

In another study, microplastics were detected in the semen and urine of all of 113 tested men from China.

Researchers broke down plastic type and how they affected sperm quality.

The most common came from packaging (polystyrene, polypropylene, and polyethylene).

PTFE, the synthetic polymer used in non-stick Teflon pans, proved the most lethal, creating 11% lower sperm concentration and 9% fewer total sperm.

Ten studies have measured microplastics in human semen. Five found 100% detection.

The rest from 84% down to 37%, but older tests used standard infrared microscopes that are blind to particles smaller than 10–20 microns. Newer studies used Raman spectroscopy, which can spot particles down to 1 micron.

So in short, 100% prevalence is plausible if not likely.

Charlene Andersen never set out to become a carnivore icon. She simply wanted her life back.
By the time she married Joe in August 1998, years of unexplained illness had piled up: severe fatigue, depression, chronic pain, trichotillomania, amenorrhea, and Lyme-related symptoms that doctors couldn’t resolve. Conventional advice and restrictive diets hadn’t helped. So the couple did something radical for the era—they eliminated everything that seemed to cause trouble and started with meat and water. It wasn’t an experiment in optimization. It was survival.
Healing wasn’t instant, but it was real. Once animal fat became her primary fat source, her cycle returned within weeks. Over time the pain eased, energy stabilized, and symptoms that had defined her life for decades began to fade. She carried two healthy pregnancies on the diet, had straightforward home births, and breastfed both boys. For years the family kept the approach private while raising their sons. Charlene refined what worked—mostly fatty ribeye and other fresh beef cuts, minimal extras—and stuck with it.
Nearly 28 years later, at 53, she is still thriving on essentially the same simple approach. She coaches, shares her experience, and has recently returned to something she loved as a younger woman: roller skating. The wobbles and falls are part of it, but so is the pure joy of movement and losing track of time. Weekly videos capture the lightness and freedom that once felt impossible.
Her story is one of the longest continuous real-world examples of a zero-carb, animal-based diet. No supplements, no plant foods, no special protocols—just consistent nourishment that let her body recover and keep going. Doctors never saw this coming because the solution sat outside the usual playbook. Charlene simply kept eating the food that worked and lived the life that followed.

Brand-New Advance Article: Functional HDL Can Neutralize the Atherogenic Power of ApoB

A freshly published advance article in the European Journal of Preventive Cardiology (DOI 10.1093/eurjpc/zwag400) shifts the focus from simple HDL cholesterol numbers to the type of HDL particles and how they interact with ApoB-containing lipoproteins.
Here is the story:

For decades, clinicians have treated ApoB (the protein that carries LDL and other atherogenic particles) as the primary driver of plaque. Every ApoB particle can enter the artery wall, become oxidized, and fuel atherosclerosis. HDL was viewed as a generic counterweight. This new analysis argues that the specific form of HDL matters far more than the total amount.

When HDL remodeling works properly, functional particles efficiently accept cholesterol from cells and from ApoB lipoproteins themselves via reverse cholesterol transport. This process can strip cholesterol from ApoB particles, reduce their residence time in the artery wall, and lower their ability to form foam cells and plaque. In other words, the right kind of HDL actively diminishes the atherosclerotic potential of ApoB.

The paper highlights the opposite situation: remodeling-derived pre-β1 HDL and remnant HDL particles generated by hepatic lipase and CETP. These are metabolically impaired forms. They do not clear cholesterol effectively. As a result, ApoB particles retain more of their cholesterol load, linger longer, and drive greater inflammation and plaque growth. The presence of these dysfunctional HDL particles is a marker that the protective interaction between HDL and ApoB has broken down.

The central conclusion is practical. ApoB sets the stage for atherosclerosis, but the functional quality of HDL can substantially blunt or amplify that risk. Measuring or improving the type of HDL—rather than chasing total HDL cholesterol—offers a clearer picture of true residual risk and a more precise target for prevention.
This is a brand-new advance publication, reflecting the latest thinking on why some people with similar ApoB levels develop very different amounts of plaque.

hits.text:
Okinawa and Blue Zone Fraud!

They sold the world a fairy tale: the Okinawans lived past 100 because they barely touched meat and lived on purple sweet potatoes. Netflix posters, books, and diet gurus all pointed to the same numbers—roughly 69% of calories from sweet potatoes, animal foods under 4%, and meat down around 3 grams a day. It was held up as proof that a near-plant diet was the secret to extreme longevity.

The catch is when those numbers were actually collected.

The Battle of Okinawa in 1945 wiped out livestock along with much of the island. Before the war, Okinawa had more than 100,000 pigs. Over 90% of farming households kept them. Pork was a cultural staple—used in daily cooking, festivals, and rituals, with every part of the animal utilized. After the fighting, the pig population collapsed to a few thousand or fewer. Households that once raised pigs were left with almost none.

The surveys that produced the famous “traditional Okinawan diet” numbers were taken around 1949–1950, right in the middle of that scarcity. What the occupation authorities recorded was a temporary post-war diet forced by destroyed herds and disrupted agriculture, not the diet the long-lived cohorts had grown up eating for decades before the war. Those centenarians were born before 1940. Their formative years and much of adult life occurred when pigs were common and pork was a normal part of the food culture.

Once herds recovered, meat intake rose again. Later generations westernized further under U.S. influence. The low-meat snapshot was frozen in time and marketed as ancient wisdom.

Age records were also badly disrupted by the same war—many destroyed, others reconstructed by occupation staff working across language and calendar differences. The clean plant-based longevity story never fully matched the historical record. The data most often cited for the Blue Zone diet in Okinawa were collected after the pigs were gone. That makes the central claim unreliable.

The popular version of the Okinawa story is not a careful reading of the evidence. It is a selective snapshot taken at the worst possible moment, then turned into a global diet prescription.
hits.draft_en:
Shawn Baker on the Okinawa Blue Zone story: the famous numbers of 69% sweet potato and barely any meat were collected after World War II, when the Battle of Okinawa had wiped out the pigs.

Before the war the island had more than 100,000 pigs, and pork was a staple in daily cooking.

When someone sells you a diet off one famous study, it's worth asking when and how the numbers were collected.

The Forest Laws Never Ended

After 1066, William the Conqueror and the Norman kings turned vast stretches of England into royal forest. Inside those bounds the red deer and fallow deer belonged to the crown. 

A peasant who killed one to feed his family could lose his eyes, his hands, his manhood, or his life. The laws were written so that, as one chronicler put it, the English would have “nothing but their eyes to weep with.”

The meat of the wild was reserved for the ruling class. Everyone else was expected to live on what the land under the plow could produce: grain, pottage, the occasional chicken or pig if they were lucky. When the Charter of the Forest finally arrived in 1217 it removed the worst mutilations and the death penalty, but the underlying idea stayed intact: the best animal protein was a privilege, not a right.

That idea never really died. It simply changed costume.
Today the same hierarchy reappears in softer language. Elite tables still feature steak, lamb, and game. Private jets still carry foie gras and dry-aged beef to conferences where the speakers tell everyone else that livestock are the problem. 

The recommended diet for the rest of the population is heavy on “whole” grains, legumes, and plant protein—foods that historically filled the peasant bowl while the lords kept the animals. The rhetoric is climate, health, or equity. The practical result is the same as the old forest law: the high-quality meat stays upstream.

The punishments are no longer blinding and castration. They are subsidies, guidelines, school menus, and social pressure. But the direction of the flow has not changed. The deer still belongs to the people who write the rules. The rest are told the grain is good for them.

Fennec foxes are desert canids whose wild diet is ~90% animal matter: insects, small rodents, reptiles, birds, eggs, and occasional plants they dig up. The Cochrane review that quietly undercuts the fruit-and-vegetable miracle story
In 2013, a team of researchers set out to answer a simple question: if you get people to eat more fruits and vegetables, does it actually prevent heart attacks, strokes, or early death? They turned to the Cochrane Collaboration, the gold standard for systematic reviews of randomized trials, and looked only at studies designed for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease.

What they found was almost nothing.
Ten trials, just 1,730 people total. Some gave people fruit or vegetables (usually a single type). Others simply told them to eat more. Follow-up was short—weeks to a few months at most. Not a single trial reported a heart attack, stroke, cancer diagnosis, or death. The studies were too brief and too small to measure those outcomes. The authors stated it plainly: none of the trials were long enough to examine effects on cardiovascular events.

What the trials did measure were intermediate markers. Advice to eat more produce produced a modest drop in systolic blood pressure of about 3 mmHg, based on just two trials. Giving people the food itself showed no clear benefit on blood pressure or cholesterol. Side effects were minor and unremarkable.

The review’s conclusion was restrained but unmistakable: there is very little evidence from randomized trials that simply increasing fruit and vegetable intake, without other dietary or lifestyle changes, prevents cardiovascular disease. More trials are needed.

That is the entire hard-outcome story from the highest-quality evidence available. No data on longevity. No data on cancer. No data on actual heart attacks or strokes. The large reductions in disease and death that are routinely attributed to “5 a day” come from observational studies, not from the randomized experiments that can isolate cause and effect.

The Cochrane review remains one of the clearest statements in the literature: when you demand the kind of evidence that matters for hard clinical outcomes, the fruit-and-vegetable prescription has almost none.

The King of Chefs Who Built Empires on Butter and Cream

In the glittering salons of Napoleonic Paris, one man turned sauce into strategy. Marie-Antoine Carême, the abandoned street child who became “the king of chefs and the chef of kings,” did not merely cook for the powerful—he rewrote the rules of French cooking around fat. 

Working for Talleyrand, the diplomat who used banquets as weapons, Carême created the mother sauces that still define haute cuisine: béchamel, velouté, espagnole, and allemande. These were not delicate broths. They began with butter-and-flour roux, simmered in rich stocks, and finished with heavy cream, egg yolks, and more butter. Allemande was a velouté enriched with cream and yolks until it shone. Béchamel was milk thickened with butter, then often enriched further. Dishes arrived at the table swimming in velvet sauces that carried flavor the way architecture carries weight—Carême himself compared pastry to architecture, and his sauces were the load-bearing walls.

Napoleon commissioned him for the wedding cake of his marriage to Marie-Louise; Talleyrand relied on him to soften foreign dignitaries. The food was unapologetically rich. Butter was not a garnish. It was the medium.

Decades later, epidemiologists noticed something that still confounds simple diet rules: the French Paradox. Populations that ate substantial amounts of saturated fat from butter, cream, and cheese showed lower rates of coronary heart disease than expected compared with other countries consuming similar levels of animal fat. 

Traditional French cooking, the kind Carême codified, was built on those same fats. Observational data from the late 20th century repeatedly showed France with relatively low CHD mortality despite high dairy-fat intake. Portion size, meal structure, and lifestyle played roles, but the core observation held: heavy use of butter and cream in classical French cuisine did not produce the heart-disease epidemic the fat-heart hypothesis predicted.

Carême died at 49, likely from years over charcoal stoves, but the sauces he systematized outlived him. They remain a living argument that the fats of traditional French cooking were not the villains later theory made them out to be.

A Lancet study tracked 505 people who went on to get type 2 diabetes, with measurements going back up to 13 years before diagnosis.

Many Americans are trying to make better choices and big-food is actively making this difficult by making the Ingredient List very difficult to read. This would be an easy fix...

1. Increase Font Size
Current Regulation: Minimum font size is 1/16 inch (1.6 mm).
Recommended Change: Increase the minimum font size to at least 1/8 inch (3.2 mm) or a point size equivalent of 12 points, which aligns with accessibility guidelines for printed materials.
Reason: Research shows that many older adults, individuals with presbyopia, and those with low vision struggle with smaller font sizes. Larger fonts improve legibility across demographics.

2. Improve Contrast Requirements
Current Regulation: Text must contrast with the background, but no specific standards are defined.
Recommended Change: Implement a minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1, as per the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) for readability.
Reason: A defined contrast standard ensures that text is distinguishable from the background, benefiting individuals with visual impairments.

3. Mandate Clear Typography
Current Regulation: No restrictions on font style.
Recommended Change: Require sans-serif fonts (e.g., Arial, Verdana) and avoid decorative or stylized typefaces.
Reason: Simple, clear fonts enhance readability, particularly for people with dyslexia or cognitive impairments.

4. Allow Dynamic Labeling Adjustments for Smaller Packages
Current Regulation: Labels on packages smaller than 12 square inches can use reduced font sizes.
Recommended Change: Require the use of fold-out labels, QR codes to provide legible ingredient information without reducing font size.
Reason: Smaller font sizes compromise accessibility; alternate methods preserve readability while accommodating limited space.

5. Use Plain Language
Current Regulation: Ingredient lists must use common or usual names but may still include scientific terminology.
Recommended Change: Mandate plain language descriptions alongside technical names (e.g., "sodium chloride (salt)").
Reason: Simplifying terms ensures greater comprehension for individuals with low literacy skills.

6. Standardize Allergen Formatting
Current Regulation: Allergens can be declared in the ingredient list or a separate "Contains" statement.
Recommended Change: Require a consistent allergen section in bold or highlighted text, clearly separated from the main ingredient list.
Reason: Improves visibility for people specifically looking for allergen information.

7. Add Digital Accessibility
Current Regulation: Labels are static with no interactive features.
Recommended Change: Encourage the use of QR codes or NFC technology on packaging to link to accessible digital formats (e.g., larger text, audio descriptions).
Reason: Provides enhanced accessibility options for individuals with disabilities.
